title: Home from Babylon: Rebuilding Jerusalem
lead: Seventy years of captivity do not mean that God has forgotten His people. What has lain in ruins for years can be rebuilt.
questions: What in your life has lain in ruins so long that you have stopped believing it can be rebuilt, and which stretch of wall is closest to your own house?
Do you let weeping and joy sound together in your rebuilding, or do you make yourself choose one?
What matter should you start “drawing the bow” for in prayer right now, so that when the decisive moment comes you can loose a “well-aimed arrow”?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: After seventy years, ruin stops being a wound and becomes simply the way things are. And then “the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia.” Cyrus issues a decree of return, just as Jeremiah had foretold, and the temple vessels carried off by one pagan king are handed back by another. History never slipped out of the Creator’s hands for a moment. Those who go back are “everyone whose spirit God had stirred”: they leave settled lives behind to go and live among the rubble. Hope is sometimes exactly that: not a feeling, but a move toward the ruins.

When the foundations of the new temple were laid, the old men who remembered the first one wept loudly and the young shouted for joy, until “the people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping.” And no one hushed anyone. That is the sound of every real rebuilding: whoever raises a marriage, a faith, or a community out of the rubble will hear both voices inside at once, and both belong. Ninety years later Nehemiah, the king’s cupbearer, heard that Jerusalem’s walls still lay in ruins. He wept, fasted, and prayed for four months, reminding God of His promises. And when the king asked what he wanted, he “prayed to the God of heaven and answered the king.” It is one of the shortest prayers in the Bible. We don’t know its words, but four months of weeping, fasting, and prayer had gone before it.

The wall was then rebuilt not by professionals but by families: priests, goldsmiths, merchants, even the daughters of Shallum, each at the stretch nearest home. Great ruins are not lifted by one hero, but by many ordinary people, each at their own few yards of wall. When mockery and threats came, they worked with one hand and held a weapon in the other. To four invitations that were really an ambush, Nehemiah replied: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down.” There is work you do not interrupt. The wall stood after fifty-two days, and the enemies “realized that this task had been accomplished by our God.” If something in your life has lain in ruins for years, it has not expired. It is enough to start with one stretch of wall.

Seventy years is a whole lifetime. People who as children had watched Jerusalem burn died in Babylon as old men, and their grandchildren knew the homeland only from stories. After that long, ruin stops being a wound and becomes simply the way things are: no one remembers anymore that it was ever different. Today’s story is about a God whose memory is better than ours. And about the fact that rebuilding what has lain in rubble for decades is possible; it just looks different from what we dreamed of.

sections.heading: A Pagan King’s Spirit Stirred
paragraphs: Everything begins with a sentence that lays the foundation for the theology of both of today’s stories: “In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia.” Babylon, which had destroyed Jerusalem, has itself just fallen, and the new ruler of the world issues a decree: whoever belongs to the LORD’s people, “may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel.” Jeremiah had foretold seventy years of captivity, and Isaiah, long before Cyrus was born, had called him by name as the one who would carry out God’s plans. Archaeology has added its own footnote: the clay Cyrus Cylinder has survived, and on it the king describes his policy of sending deported peoples home and rebuilding their temples. The grand politics of an empire turned out to be a tool in God’s hand, through which a small, conquered nation returned to its homeland. There is one more detail in this scene, and it closes the bracket of the exile: Cyrus returns the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem. One pagan king took them; another gave them back. Through all that time, history never slipped out of God’s hands for a moment.

sections.heading: Those Whose Spirit Was Stirred
paragraphs: The decree opened the way for everyone, but the text is clear: the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, the priests and the Levites set out, “everyone whose spirit God had stirred.” Not everyone. After seventy years, Babylon had become home: there were businesses there, gardens, the graves of loved ones, a whole settled life. Many stayed, and yesterday’s reading about Esther showed that God did not turn His back on those who chose to stay in exile. Those who got up made a decision that was crazy from a human point of view: to leave the prosperity of the empire and travel some six hundred miles to go and live among the rubble. Sometimes hope takes exactly this shape: not a feeling, but a move. You pack up your life and set out toward the ruins, because you have come to believe they matter. The archaeology of the Persian period shows a gradual rebuilding of settlement in Judah. People who had come to live on rubble did not put together something makeshift to wait things out. They built as if they believed in a future that would last for generations. That is how you can tell whether someone has really come back.

sections.heading: Weeping and Joy in One Voice
paragraphs: Once they have arrived and the first months have passed, the settlers lay the foundations of a new temple. The priests stand in their vestments with trumpets, the Levites with cymbals, and all of them sing a song still known in Israel today: “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever.” And then comes one of the truest scenes in the whole Bible: “But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully. The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping.” The old men wept because they remembered that house and could see this one would be humbler. The young shouted for joy because for the first time in their lives they were watching something in Jerusalem begin rather than end. And no one hushed anyone. That is the sound of every real rebuilding: after years of ruin, the new is never simply the old come back. Whoever rebuilds a marriage, a faith, their health, or a community will hear both voices inside at once: grief for what is gone for good, and joy over what is beginning. The Bible says both belong. Out of just such a mix of weeping and singing, God knows how to build.

sections.heading: The Cupbearer Who Wept for Four Months
paragraphs: Ninety years later, the walls of Jerusalem still lie in ruins. The temple stands, but the city is defenseless and half empty. The news reaches the Persian court and Nehemiah, the king’s Jewish cupbearer: “The remnant who survived the exile are there in the province, in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire.” The reaction of a high-ranking imperial official: “I sat down and wept. I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven.” The book’s calendar reveals that about four months passed between that news and his conversation with the king. Four months of prayer from a man who could not yet do anything. The content of these pleas, preserved in the book, is woven, sentence by sentence, out of the five books of Moses: Nehemiah reminds God of His own words about scattering His people for unfaithfulness and gathering those who return. He does not improvise. He prays the promises the Creator Himself signed, and holds Him to His word. That is the strongest kind of prayer the Bible knows. Then the king notices his sadness and asks: “What is your request?” And here comes my favorite sentence in the book: “So I prayed to the God of heaven and answered the king.” Between the ruler’s question and the courtier’s answer lies one of the shortest prayers in the Bible. We do not know its words; we only know that Nehemiah prayed in a split second. Yet that arrow flew true because it had four months of drawing the bow behind it. That is how prayer works for people who are suddenly handed their moment: lightning-fast on the outside, long on the inside. Nehemiah, like Esther yesterday, stood high up at a pagan court at exactly the moment his people needed someone in those circles.

sections.heading: Let Us Start Rebuilding
paragraphs: Nehemiah arrives in Jerusalem and at first says nothing. At night, on a donkey, he rides around the ruins, taking in the scale of the disaster before saying a word about it. Then he calls the leaders together, and instead of a lecture he gives a testimony: he tells them how the good God had watched over him and what the king had said. The answer comes back: “Let us start rebuilding.” And “they set their hands to this good work.” Chapter 3 of the book is a long list, dull at first glance, of the people who repaired the walls. Yet it is this list that tells us how the walls were rebuilt. The work was done by priests and goldsmiths, perfumers and merchants, people from the surrounding towns, and even the daughters of a man named Shallum, among the few women in the Bible involved in building work. Almost none of them were masons. Each one took the section nearest their own house. Throughout the chapter, like a refrain, one Hebrew verb meaning “to strengthen” comes back more than thirty times. Not “they raised it from scratch,” but “they strengthened”: they took what had survived and gave it back its strength. Rebuilding rarely starts from an empty lot. More often it starts from remnants that can still be strengthened. Great ruins are rebuilt not by the great effort of one hero, but by a hundred families, each strengthening its own piece. This is a lesson for churches too: the renewal of a community does not come through one outstanding person, but through many ordinary ones, each standing at their own few yards of wall.

sections.heading: One Hand on the Work, a Weapon in the Other
paragraphs: Rebuilding immediately draws opposition. Sanballat, the governor of Samaria, a man also known from papyri outside the Bible, first mocks, then threatens armed attack, and among the people discouragement finds its voice: “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” Anyone who has taken on a big rebuilding knows that moment: the enthusiasm has drained away, and the rubble seems to have grown. Nehemiah answers with organization and prayer at the same time: “The laborers who carried materials worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other,” guards kept watch through the night, and no one took off their clothes. And when his enemies four times invite him to a “meeting” in the valley that is meant to cost him his life, he answers with a sentence that ought to hang over the desk of anyone doing something important: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?” Not every provocation deserves an answer. Not every invitation has to be accepted. There is work you do not interrupt. Nor does the danger come only from outside. Inside the besieged community the poor raised an outcry: better-off brothers were lending to them at interest, and they were pledging their fields, their vineyards, and finally their own children. Nehemiah rebuked the leaders publicly and made them give back what had been pledged, and for twelve years as governor he himself did not take the allowance due to him from taxes, so as not to add to the people’s burden. He knew that a wall of stone would not protect a city that was devouring itself from within. Rebuilding the walls and rebuilding justice must go hand in hand, or neither of them would make any sense. And the wall stands: “the wall was completed in fifty-two days.” The enemies, Nehemiah notes, “were afraid and disheartened, for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God.” A wall built by the trembling hands of amateurs became proof of God’s providence. The celebration afterward was worthy of the building: two great thanksgiving choirs processed along the top of the wall in opposite directions until they met at the temple, and the joy of Jerusalem, so the record says, could be heard far away. They sang on a wall that not long before had been a heap of rubble. There is no better pulpit for a song of thanks than a rebuilt ruin.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If something in your life has lain in ruins for years, so long that you have stopped even grieving over it, this story tells you three things. First: seventy years of ruin did not erase Jerusalem from God’s memory. Your rubble has not expired either. Second: the rebuilding will begin not with a miracle but with a decision to get up and head toward the rubble, and it will sound like weeping and joy at once. Don’t be ashamed of either voice. Third: take the stretch of wall nearest your own house. Not the whole wall, just one stretch. As a community, let us draw two lessons from this story. Renewal is carried not by one hero but by many families, each working on its own stretch. And every good rebuilding will draw scoffers, who need no answer other than Nehemiah’s: I am doing a great work and cannot come down.
